blocks: Watch for both failure modes: the settled routine that stopped looking, and the endless survey that never commits.

Seen through cybernetics, a learner is a regulator holding a course through an environment it can only partly see. Exploitation is the corrective action along the known heading. Exploration is the sampling that keeps the map of the environment current, so the corrections stay pointed at the real world. Ashby's requisite variety says a regulator must carry at least as many responses as the world has disturbances, and exploration is how it acquires the variety it lacks. Second-order cybernetics adds the observer to the loop: a gardener steering their own learning is regulating the system that does the steering, which is why the balance is never set once and left alone.

My/Principle/Learn/in Public frames knowledge gardening as calibrating these two forces: exploring adds new things to the garden and new connections to the world, and exploiting tends what is already planted so it becomes more vibrant and real. Explore and Exploit each have a page of their own.
Choosing to exploit means taking the option that present knowledge says pays best, and collecting the reward.
Gains — reward now, with little variance: refinement, efficiency, execution, and the compounding that comes from doing the known thing well.
Costs — the information forgone: untried options stay unknown, and the estimate of the current best goes unchallenged. The map stops being updated while the world keeps changing.

Too far — the settled routine: an agent locked onto the best option it happened to find early, a firm polishing a product after the market has left, a garden that is only ever pruned and never planted.
Choosing to explore means spending a turn on an option whose payoff is unknown, to learn what it is worth.

Gains — information: a truer map of which options pay, and the chance of finding something better than the current best. The value is highest early, when little is known and a long horizon remains to use what is learned.
Costs — the reward forgone on that turn, since the known best was passed over, plus the chance that the unknown option is worse. Returns arrive late and uncertain.

Too far — the perpetual survey: an agent, team or gardener that keeps sampling and never settles, so nothing learned is ever cashed in. March described the result as too many undeveloped ideas and too little distinctive competence.

Team-based agents mark a shift from single-player AI tools—assistants that serve one person, like a personal chief of staff—to agents that act as shared teammates inside a team's existing communication channels, per AI/Concept/Multiplayer/Log/26/09/21 Mon Readwise Summary of Claude Tag.
Instead of living in a private chat with one user, the agent sits at the intersection where a team already comes together: a shared channel that every relevant person can see and add to.

Persistent teammates in Slack carry the whole history of a channel, so no individual has to brief them from scratch. One person's agent-assisted work hands off cleanly to the next person, because the agent's memory of the thread is continuous rather than scoped to a single conversation.

Claude/Tag is Anthropic's instance of this pattern: @-mentioning it in a Slack thread summons a version of Claude that is not tied to any one person, running instead as an organization-scoped teammate with its own permissions, tool access, and persistent memory.

CursorAI/Cloud Agent applies the same pattern to software delivery: mentioning the agent in a Slack channel kicks off work on a collaborative development surface that the whole channel can watch, rather than one developer's private editor.
Org-scoped identity, not personal — permissions, tool access, and memory attach to the team or organization, not to whichever individual happens to type the @-mention.
The conversation is the interface — work happens inside the channel; agents call APIs and run commands in the background, surfacing only the approvals and decisions a human needs to see.
Bounded initiative — a multiplayer agent can take initiative by following up on quiet threads, flagging relevant information, and managing long-horizon tasks without being re-prompted each time.
Division of labor — agents take on the stable, repeatable layers of work, while humans hold the creative and strategic end of the judgment.
Invocation is an @-mention inside an existing channel (@Claude, @cursor) rather than a switch to a separate app; the agent reads the thread it is tagged in for context.

Specialized coworker agents narrow the same pattern to a functional role: an editorial team's agent named Andy collects "nuggets" of story ideas from Slack threads and turns them into newsletter drafts; an always-on product-manager agent keeps a memory.md file tracking priorities and tags a human only when their input is needed.

At company scale, this becomes part of a broader move toward headless software—Salesforce and Slack describe positioning themselves as an agentic OS—where work happens inside the conversation instead of a separate dashboard login.
Claude/Tag handling incident response, bug triage, and shipping code directly from a Slack thread.

CursorAI/Cloud Agent kicking off an investigation from a Slack message, tagging people for input, and producing a PR-ready artifact visible to everyone in the channel; Anthropic reported that 65% of one product team's code now originates from Slack-triggered workflows.
Andy and the always-on product-manager agent, applying the same pattern to editorial and product-management roles rather than engineering.
Not a personal assistant shared by copy-pasting a login: a multiplayer agent needs its own org-scoped permissions and continuous channel memory, independent of any one person's session.
Not confined to chat: the agent calls APIs and runs commands in the background; the channel is the approval and notification surface, not the whole of its work.

Coined by Chroma research in Chroma/Paper/25/07/Context Rot - Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
Context rot is the degradation of an AI/LLM's performance as input length grows, caused by its non-uniform and unreliable handling of extended context.

LLMs have a "context window" that is determined by a maximum number of input Tokens. For a given model, this window affects the upper bound of the complexity of the problem they can handle as well as the amount of private business data that can be utilized in a query.
